openbsdDesktop: ↶ Home Field Manual OBS-7 · desktop values that survive OpenBSD for Desktops The default install guards the machine like a server. A desktop needs the same discipline with roomier ceilings — enough that Firefox plays a video while the system keeps answering, without a single change that cannot be undone by deleting one line. sysctl · sndiod · firefox · wsconsctl · apm vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies every knob is reversible 01 The deal The stock values of a fresh install are chosen to protect machines you never look at. That is why a browser can open too many files and fail, or a media pipeline can exhaust the process ceiling while the desktop crawls. The project itself documents this: the values exist so a runaway service eats the “small” quota first. The deal you are signing when you keep reading: Reversibility first. Most of this page is sysctl at runtime. Reboot clears it if you regret it. Persistence is a plain-text line in /etc/sysctl.conf — remove the line, the value is gone. No recompiled kernels, no -current, no patches. Everything here works on the release you already installed, with the packages the mirrors already serve. No fancy filesystems, no exotic schedulers. The default FFS layout stays; the default services stay. A desktop is the place you should be least creative. Firefox does the media work ; the OS only has to stop tripping it. Note: check every number against your own machine ( sysctl -a prints the current ones). The kernel clamps or rejects values outside its range, and it tells you when it does — listen to it, do not fight it. 02 The values that stop the lag This is the section you came for. Three ceilings cover most desktop slowdowns: file descriptors, the process cap, and the thread cap. A browser is many processes each holding many files when video is rolling; the defaults were sized smaller than that. Sysctl Desktop value Default-ish base Why video lagged kern.maxfiles 10240 7022 Each tab/thread keeps sockets, pipes, media descriptors; the cap lands and the browser queues instead of rendering. kern.maxproc 65000 1310 A modern browser spawns processes per tab. Past the cap, new tabs die or the compositor stalls. kern.maxthread 4096 1024 Media decoding is thread-hungry; when threads get refused, video decodes late — which is the “OS lagging” feel. Apply them live, right now, no reboot: $ doas sysctl kern.maxfiles=10240 $ doas sysctl kern.maxproc=65000 $ doas sysctl kern.maxthread=4096 Then open Firefox, play a video, resize the window, switch tabs. The machine should stay smooth because the browser stopped knocking on a closed ceiling. If a value is refused “Invalid argument” or “Permission denied” , the range on your kernel is different — back off, or read options(4) ; do not shave the kernel. What I am not telling you to change: vm.* percentages, buffer cache ratios, kern.maxclusters beyond sanity, scheduler hacks. On a general-purpose laptop those defaults are right, and turning them is how people “tune” a working system into a mysterious one. Seriously, only three sysctls? For video playback without OS lag, yes in the common case: descriptors, processes and threads are what a browser exhausts first. If your case is different, the evidence is readable: systat vmstat during playback shows you whether the machine is swapping (RAM problem → section 06), starving on descriptors (files problem → this section), or neither (then the lag is mismatched driver rendering → section 04). 03 Testing, then keeping The beauty of sysctls: try, keep, or leave with a one-line difference. Runtime first as above; then, to survive reboots, the same key=value pairs go into /etc/sysctl.conf : # /etc/sysctl.conf — one line each, no 'sysctl' keyword kern.maxfiles=10240 kern.maxproc=65000 kern.maxthread=4096 Confirm the boot result once: $ doas reboot $ sysctl kern.maxfiles kern.maxproc kern.maxthread Discipline that keeps this safe for a normal user: Change one thing at a time and use the machine for an hour. If anything feels strange, delete one line from /etc/sysctl.conf , reboot, done. Keep a note (this page's checklist, or a file) of every line you added. Six months from now “the system changed behaviour” will actually be “past-me added a line”. Do not set values you have no reason for. More is not smoother; mis-sized memory pools are just a new way to be slow. 04 Firefox, tamed Firefox from packages is the right Firefox — it is built against the system's libraries and speaks sndio for audio natively: $ doas pkg_add firefox Video playback on OpenBSD decodes in software through the bundled ffmpeg stack; the machine behind sections 02 and 06 is what makes it smooth. There is one optional forward step: Note (optional): on machines whose DRM driver exposes hardware video decode (newer Intel graphics are the usual candidates), Firefox can attempt VAAPI: about:config → media.ffmpeg.vaapi.enabled → true , restart, and check whether videos actually behave. It is per-profile and revertible with the same switch set back to false . If there is no improvement — or video gets worse — flip it back and move on. No loss. Warn: do not chase acceleration through unofficial builds, forks or scripts pasted from forums. A browser that runs outside the package system is un-signed, un-updated and a genuine security regression on the machine you can least afford to regress. Small habits that keep it fast Keep the profile small: hundreds of dormant tabs cost memory on any OS. Let the package system update it ( pkg_add -u ) instead of living between versions. If the browser itself freezes but the desktop answers, that is an in-browser problem — sections 02/06 will not fix a broken profile; a fresh one will. 05 Audio without crackle sndiod is already running and mixing by default. Desktops rarely need tuning; when video + music at once hiss or crackle under load, the device buffer can grow a little: # /etc/rc.conf.local — only if audio crackles under load sndiod_flags=-b2400 $ doas rcctl set sndiod flags -b2400 $ doas rcctl restart sndiod Bigger buffer = more latency (a few milliseconds you will not notice) in exchange for staying fluid when the CPU spikes. Defaults first; change only what crackles. Per-application volume just works on sndio ; per-app mixers from other systems do not exist here and are not missed. Note: if audio devices change (plug/unplug, monitors with speakers), sndiod re-reads devices on the fly. Persistent weirdness is usually the volume knob of the wrong device, not broken config. 06 RAM arithmetic No sysctl rescues too little RAM. Video in a browser is a few gigabytes of anonymous memory; the page daemon starts clawing pages back as soon as the machine is tight, and that reclaiming is the real “OS is lagging” experience — the system keeps running while it swaps your video in and out. $ systat vm 1 # watch pi/po (pages in/out) during a video 8 GB : fine for one browser session + WM + terminal. 16 GB : the comfortable desktop number. How to be honest about it: play your worst case (video + video call + editor) and watch systat vm . If pi/po churn while the system feels mushy, you need more memory, not more tuning. Swap exists to exist, not to be a second RAM: leave the default swap sized at install time, leave the virtual-memory ratios alone, and treat “ vm.anonmin ”-style advice as something for people with a measurement, not a feeling. Note: if the machine is old-slow rather than out-of-memory, upgrade path is RAM → SSD → patient browser habits. The sysctls of section 02 only remove the artificial ceiling. 07 Trackpads and keyboards These are wsconsctl knobs — same reversibility as sysctls. Trackpad tapping and natural scrolling behaviour live here: $ doas wsconsctl -w mouse.tapping=1 # tap = click, live $ doas wsconsctl -w mouse.scrolling=0 # 0 traditional, 1 natural And to keep them after reboot, /etc/wsconsctl.conf takes the bare key=value lines: # /etc/wsconsctl.conf mouse.tapping=1 mouse.scrolling=0 Keyboard layouts follow the same pattern; list what your console understands and set it live with wsconsctl keyboard.map= ... then persist in the same file. Two knobs on the laptop (tapping + scrolling) cover 90% of the “OpenBSD feels unfinished” first impressions. Warn: do not autoload random X11 driver flags or modeline hacks from forums to fix a trackpad. The wsconsctl route is the project's own and it survives xenodm restarts; the forum route survives nothing. 08 Battery, lid, suspend Laptops get the pleasant part of OpenBSD: suspend ( zzz ) works out of the box, and the lid action is a sysctl: $ apm # battery state + performance mode $ doas apm -A # automatic performance adjustment $ doas sysctl machdep.lidaction=1 # close lid = suspend (1); 0 leaves it alone Persist the lid behaviour in /etc/sysctl.conf like the others: # /etc/sysctl.conf machdep.lidaction=1 Allow yourself to suspend without a password being typed each time — acceptable only for zzz itself: # /etc/doas.conf permit nopass :wheel cmd zzz Warn: permit nopass otherwise gets you a root-shaped hole in the name of convenience. One command, exactly that command. Note: after suspend, if the clock is off, ntpd re-syncs automatically. If keys repeat weirdly until the next reboot, that is your machine's firmware being ancient, not OpenBSD's fault alone — the same happens walking between three other OSes. 09 A window manager that answers cwm ships in base and is the truthful answer to “what WM on OpenBSD”. X as a whole is started by xenodm : $ doas rcctl enable xenodm $ doas rcctl start xenodm And your ~/.xsession simply must point at it (this file is the only thing between you and a black screen; keep it tiny): # ~/.xsession . /etc/X11/xinit/xinitrc.d/40-systray 2>/dev/null || true xsetroot -solid \"#070b12\" exec cwm Why cwm and not something showier: it is keyboard-first, memory-flat, updated with the base system, and sports the most honest manual page in any WM. Window managers from packages (fvwm, i3 and so on) also work — if a package install goes wrong, it is removable and you still have twm and a console. Note: keep xenodm enabled rather than starting X from a bare console every time; multiuser discipline survives by accident otherwise. 10 Fonts and the packages worth having A desktop without good fonts is a desktop you describe as “ugly”. This is fixed by packages, and it cannot break anything: $ doas pkg_add noto-fonts noto-fonts-emoji dejavu-fonts fonts: a full family + emoji covers all web pages you will open. audio/video: nothing extra; ffmpeg rides inside Firefox and friends via packages. tools: curl , git , vim (or neovim), zsh — all from packages, all disposable. updates are one command, run occasionally: pkg_add -u . Note: stay on -release / -stable as a normal user. -current is a full-time hobby; a browser that changes under your video every week is a form of self-harm. 11 The boring parts that matter User discipline: live as a normal user; doas for the few things above. Everything on this page runs through doas, never inside a bare root shell. Email noise: the daily maintenance cron mail tells you about things like “disk nearing capacity”. Read it instead of filtering it: it is the OS whispering. /etc/motd : shorten it. Reclaiming screen inches — not “tuning”, but the daily reward. dmesg and sysctl -a : after every change, compare once before/after before calling it “better”. Feelings lie; diffs do not. Back up the small config: these are now “your” files — /etc/sysctl.conf , /etc/wsconsctl.conf , /etc/doas.conf , ~/.xsession . Four files; save a copy with tar when they feel right. Warn: nothing on this page should push you to enable services from rcctl you cannot name the purpose of. A desktop with 8 enabled daemons is a small server wearing a desktop's face, and it inherits a server's attack surface with none of its pay. 12 Cheat sheet Goal Command Un-stick video ceilings (live) doas sysctl kern.maxfiles=10240 kern.maxproc=65000 kern.maxthread=4096 Keep them over reboots same three pairs, one per line, in /etc/sysctl.conf See current values sysctl kern.maxfiles kern.maxproc kern.maxthread Audio breathing room rcctl set sndiod flags -b2400 && rcctl restart sndiod Trackpad manners doas wsconsctl -w mouse.tapping=1 (+ line in /etc/wsconsctl.conf ) Suspend now / on lid doas zzz / machdep.lidaction=1 Watch memory churn systat vm 1 X with cwm rcctl enable xenodm , exec cwm in ~/.xsession Fonts pkg_add noto-fonts noto-fonts-emoji dejavu-fonts Everything fresh pkg_add -u 13 Your desktop, checked off Progress below is stored in this browser ( localStorage ) only — closing the page keeps it. 0 / 10 RESET sysctl -a captured before any change (your before-picture) kern.maxfiles=10240 applied and kept in /etc/sysctl.conf kern.maxproc=65000 applied and kept kern.maxthread=4096 applied and kept Video in Firefox plays smoothly with tabs switching beside it systat vm watched during playback; pi/po calm (or RAM planned) Audio checked under load; -b2400 applied only if it crackled Trackpad tapping/scroll set via wsconsctl and persisted Lid + suspend + doas nopass for zzz only The four config files copied away once ( sysctl.conf , wsconsctl.conf , doas.conf , ~/.xsession )

ordersAndConscience: Home Monkey Blog · Big Dossier English Português Politics, Law & Justice · Big Dossier Orders and Conscience The same machine, seen from both sides: evil done in the name of the Good, good done in the name of evil — and what the psychology of obedience, moral injury and refusal tells us about the person inside the uniform. Obedience Refusal Moral injury De-escalation Sources Bilingual How to read this dossier You wear a uniform, 15 minutes — read 1 , 2 and 7 . The four questions in section 7 are the part worth memorising. You are a citizen, 20 minutes — read 3 , 4 and 5 . These are the two faces of the same machine, and the bill. You train people, 30 minutes — read 6 , 7 and 8 . Section 8 is the part institutions hate. You have five minutes — section 2 : the answer that the law gave in 1946 and never took back. You want the whole history — read 3 and 4 together, century by century: every order in the first list has a name in the second. 1. How obedience is manufactured No state has ever needed to convince most of its people to be cruel. It only has to arrange the situation so that cruelty looks like procedure. The rest is engineering, and the engineering has been studied for eighty years. The experiments that still explain the office Stanley Milgram's 1963 study at Yale put ordinary volunteers in front of a machine they believed delivered shocks to a stranger. A man in a grey coat said please continue . About sixty-five percent went all the way to the highest switch. When two peers openly refused, obedience collapsed to a small fraction; when the authority left the room, or was replaced by an ordinary man in a shirt, it fell sharply too. The finding was never about Germans, or about evil people: it was about how much the obedience of a normal person depends on the room he is standing in. Solomon Asch showed the same soft machinery with lines of different length: people will deny their own eyes to agree with a group. In the standard experiments about a third of answers followed the majority, and roughly three quarters of participants conformed at least once. Nobody was threatened. Being the only one who disagrees was cost enough. The Stanford prison study of 1971 is still quoted as proof that power corrupts. It should be quoted as a warning about evidence instead: recordings released decades later show coaching, rehearsed lines and a guard role played to please the researcher. The lesson survives, but inverted — a study can be built to produce the result the designer wants, which is exactly what an institution does when it dresses a decision as a policy. The four tools of distance Albert Bandura described moral disengagement as a set of switches that let a person do harm and keep a clean self-image. They appear in every bureaucracy, in every language: Moral justification — the cause is Good, therefore the act is permitted. God, nation, order, security, peace, revolution. Euphemism — pacification, collateral damage, enhanced interrogation, redistribution, cleaning the area. The word arrives before the act and hides it while it happens. Diffusion of responsibility — I do not make policy, I apply it. The signature is one of forty signatures. The order came from above, and above is a committee. Dehumanisation — they are not like us, they are a mob, they are numbers on a list, they are a risk score. A soldier , a police officer and a clerk in an office are trained in the first two and protected by the third. The fourth one is announced on the radio. Nobody starts at the grave Complicity is built in steps small enough to be deniable: deliver the message, keep the file, sign the transfer, do not ask why the list is shorter. Each step makes the next one cheaper, because refusing now would mean admitting what the previous step was. This is why the first refusal is the strongest and the last one is almost impossible. Reserve Police Battalion 101, Józefów, July 1942: the commander offered those who did not feel able to shoot the option of stepping out. Most men still killed. The ones who stepped out were not punished, were not transferred, and were not killed. Refusal was possible — that is the uncomfortable, important fact that the defence "there was no choice" cannot survive. The price of being the one who asks Against the moral cost stands a small, ordinary, human cost: transfer, mockery, no promotion, the locker room going quiet, the feeling of being the problem for the group. Armies and police forces have always known this and have used it as a free enforcement mechanism. Distrust is cheaper than discipline. The counterweights are documented too: visible identification , written records , an independent complaint route, and a chain of command that publicly protects the person who said no. The soft machine Modern obedience rarely arrives as a shout. It arrives as a screen: a risk score, a quota of fines, an automated flag, a list of names, a pushback order written in administrative language. The old sentence survives intact, only the grammar changed: I only followed orders became I only applied the rule . The distance grew from an office wall to an interface, and distance is the ingredient that does the work. 2. What the law already decided The excuse that emptied the twentieth century — Befehl ist Befehl , an order is an order — was answered in writing, with sources that any uniformed person can read in ten minutes. Nuremberg Principle IV (formulated by the UN International Law Commission, 1950): acting under the order of a government or a superior does not relieve a person of responsibility under international law, provided a moral choice was in fact possible to him . That last clause is the whole doctrine. It does not say obey is always criminal; it says obedience is not a shield. Rome Statute, article 33 (1998): superior orders are not a defence when the order is manifestly unlawful — and orders to commit genocide or crimes against humanity are, by definition, manifestly unlawful. Customary international humanitarian law, rule 155 : obeying a superior order does not relieve a subordinate of criminal responsibility if he knew the act was unlawful, or should have known. Conscience is a protected right : article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion; the UN human rights system reads conscientious objection to military service as a legitimate exercise of that right. The European Court of Human Rights said it plainly in Bayatyan v. Armenia (2011), after decades in which it had avoided the question. In Portugal , article 41(6) of the Constitution states that the right to conscientious objection is guaranteed in the terms of the law — a sentence written in 1976, two years after a war ended and a regime fell. Two honest qualifications, because a dossier that only sells comfort is useless. The first: the law protects you afterwards, sometimes. On the day, in the corridor, with a supervisor waiting for your answer, the law is not in the room. Only procedure and allies are. Section 7 is therefore about procedure, not principles. The second: "manifestly unlawful" is a higher bar than "unpleasant" or "pointless" or "politically embarrassing". An order you dislike is not an illegal order. The test is narrower than conscience and wider than rank, and it is worth learning precisely because it protects the refuser from becoming merely insubordinate. Never hand your conscience to someone else to hold. 3. Face one — evil in the name of the Good Every century repeats the same sentence: the cause is Good, therefore the act must be permitted. What follows is the file, not the sermon. Figures follow the historians and the commissions of inquiry; where estimates differ, they differ, and the difference is noted. All Before 1900 1900–1945 1945–1990 After 1990 36 / 36 1099 · Jerusalem After the walls of the First Crusade 's prize fell, the population of the city was killed in the name of God. Medieval chroniclers claimed tens of thousands; modern estimates are lower, still in the low thousands. The slaughter was described by the winners as an act of purification. 1209 · Béziers The Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars. The line kill them all, God will know his own is attributed to a papal legate and may be legend — the sack of the city was not. Crusades against Christians, once started, never paused for a theological check. 1478–1834 · Spanish Inquisition An institution built to punish belief, with a bureaucracy, a filing system, an interrogation practice and a public ceremony. Most of the accused were never executed; the machinery that made the threat credible was the point. 1492 · Spain, and 1496 · Portugal Jews expelled from Spain, then forced to convert or leave in Portugal. An administrative decision, taken in law, executed by officials, with the property of the expelled staying behind. 1885–1908 · Congo Free State Leopold II of Belgium ran a private colony as a rubber concession. Hostages were taken to force quotas; hands were cut as proof of ammunition used. Roger Casement's 1904 consular report and E. D. Morel's campaign dragged it into the light. Estimates of population loss run from one million to several million, and the disagreements are about method, not about cruelty. 1904–1908 · German South-West Africa Von Trotha's extermination order against the Herero, then the Nama. Roughly four fifths of the Herero died; the survivors were used as forced labour. Germany formally recognised the killings as genocide in 2021, and agreed to a fund of about €1.1 billion. It took 116 years, and the negotiations were with the government of a country, not with the descendants in the room. 1915 · Armenia Intellectuals arrested on 24 April, then the deportation law of May, then the marches and the killing units. An estimated 1.5 million people, out of the war 's chaos, by design. More than thirty states and the overwhelming majority of historians call it genocide; the denial continues as a state policy, which is itself part of the file. 1917 · Chemin des Dames After a failed French offensive, soldiers refused to attack again. Thousands were involved, hundreds sentenced, dozens executed. They were not traitors: they had concluded that the tactic was slaughter and that obedience was the fuel. 1918 · Kiel German sailors refused an order to sail out for a last battle they could not win. The refusal spread, the republic was declared, the war stopped. A mutiny ended what a war had started. 1932–33 · Ukraine Famine imposed by requisition and administrative orders: an estimated 3.5 to 5 million dead. It has been recognised as a genocide by a number of parliaments, including the European Parliament — recognition depends on intent, and the intent question is argued by historians, not by committees. 1933–1945 · The Holocaust Six million Jews, and the Roma, the disabled and the political prisoners beside them. The gas chamber was tested first on German patients in the T4 programme, where roughly 250,000 to 300,000 people were killed and, crucially, the paperwork, the false death certificates and the public acceptance were rehearsed. The technique travelled east in the same files. 1937 · Nanjing Weeks of mass killing and rape after the city fell, with figures argued between tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands depending on the source. The dispute over the number has been, for decades, a dispute between states. 1937–38 · Soviet Union The Great Terror, with roughly 700,000 executions recorded in the NKVD's own papers, plus the camps . Quotas were assigned to regions. When the state sets a quota, an obedient man becomes an accomplice by arithmetic. 1940 · Katyn About 22,000 Polish officers and prisoners shot, each with a bullet to the back of the head, in forests that took fifty years to be admitted. The officers were killed by state whose official account was a lie so solid that it divided Europe. 1941 · Jedwabne and Iaşi In Poland, Polish neighbours killed at least 340 Jews in July; in Romania, the Iaşi pogrom killed thousands in June. The Holocaust did not need an imported apparatus everywhere: in places, the local population did the work and the German officers watched. 1942 · Józefów The men of Reserve Police Battalion 101 — middle-aged reservists, not ideological fanatics — shot women and children in a Polish forest. Their commander offered the chance to step out. Most did not. Those who did were not punished. 1943–44 · Bulgaria and Hungary Deportations of Bulgarian Jews were stopped by protests led by Dimitar Peshev; in Hungary, hundreds of thousands were deported after the German occupation, and some were saved by diplomats with stamps. Both facts belong in the same file. 1950s · Kenya British forces fought the Mau Mau insurgency by moving up to 1.5 million Kikuyu into fortified villages and holding suspects in camps where torture was systematic. In 2013 the United Kingdom settled a case brought by survivors for £19.9 million, with a statement of regret — the only court that could rule on most of the victims had already died. 1954–1962 · Algeria French troops used torture as a method, and the method was defended in the name of the Republic's survival. General Pâris de Bollardière asked to be relieved rather than sign it. In 1960, 121 intellectuals and soldiers signed a declaration defending the right to disobey in that war. 1960 · Sharpeville A police line opened fire on a protest against pass laws: 69 dead, most shot in the back. South Africa declared a state of emergency and banned the organisations involved. The photograph of the aftermath is a form of evidence the law cannot refuse. 1965 · Indonesia After a narrative of attempted coup, the army organised the killing of alleged communists: several hundred thousand, up to a million by some estimates. Nobody was punished, and the men who did it still recount it calmly in front of cameras decades later. 1968 · My Lai American soldiers killed 504 civilians, mostly women and children, in a hamlet in Vietnam. The Army's own inquiry found the cover-up. A helicopter crew landed their machine between the troops and the people. The man who did that was called a traitor before he was called a hero. 1970 · Kent State National Guard troops shot into students protesting the war: four dead, nine wounded. The State's own commission called the shooting unjustified. Weapons in the hands of frightened men, obeying a vague request to restore order. 1973–1978 · Latin America Chile after the coup, Argentina's "dirty war" (about 30,000 disappeared, per the CONADEP report), Operation Condor — a network of dictatorships sharing lists, planes and prisoners. palavrasSubjectivas: A Impotência Ontológica do Discurso Como as palavras falham em alterar a realidade e apenas catalisam a imaginação da mente pensante 1. A Fractura entre o Nome e a Coisa Desde a génese do pensamento filosófico, a humanidade debate-se com uma ilusão persistente: a crença de que a linguagem possui uma força demiúrgica ou mágica, capaz de moldar, reconfigurar ou violar a matéria do universo. Criámos mitos onde mundos nascem da pronúncia de um verbo e onde maldições alteram a biologia dos corpos. Contudo, a física, a biologia e a ontologia rigorosa demonstram rigorosamente o oposto. As palavras são vibrações acústicas de ar deslocado ou traços de pigmento sobre superfícies; elas não possuem carga genética, massa quântica nem força gravitacional para alterar a realidade material. O axioma fundamental sobre o qual assentamos esta reflexão é inequívoco: As palavras não mudam a realidade, elas só potenciam a capacidade de imaginar, de quem tem a capacidade de pensar. Quando um enunciado é proferido, a realidade física permanece absolutamente intocada. O impacto da palavra não ocorre no mundo exterior, mas sim no interior do recetador — no vasto teatro da mente capaz de desconfiar, interpretar e projetar cenários imaginários. É no fosso entre o facto concreto e a projeção mental que a humanidade constrói os seus maiores pesadelos, conflitos e neuroses sociais. 2. A Imutabilidade do Real Perante a Palavra Para testarmos a absoluta impotência da linguagem sobre a matéria, observemos enunciados de diferente amplitude conceitual e o modo como o universo físico responde a cada um deles: Exemplo 1: Impotência sobre a Biologia Enunciado: "Os elefantes têm asas." A Realidade Física: Ao proferir ou escrever esta frase, nenhum paquiderme na savana africana ou indiana sofreu qualquer mutação genética. As suas escápulas não desenvolveram ossos pneumáticos, não surgiram penas ou membranas, nem a força da gravidade deixou de exercer tração sobre o seu corpo de várias toneladas. O elefante permanece rigorosamente sem asas. A palavra falhou em alterar a biologia, mas na mente de quem escuta e pensa, acende-se uma imagem surrealista: um elefante a planar nos céus. Exemplo 2: Impotência sobre o Transcendente Enunciado: "Deus é homossexual." A Realidade Física/Metafísica: O conceito de Divindade — quer seja interpretado como a totalidade do cosmos, a causa primordial ou um ser metafísico — permanece absolutamente inalterado por categorias de orientação sexual humanas criadas no século XIX. Se Deus existe, a Sua natureza substancial não é reconfigurada por uma afirmação verbal; se não existe, o vazio não ganha atributos biológicos. A palavra não toca a essência divina; contudo, na mente do crente ou do teólogo, o enunciado desencadeia uma tempestade de projeções morais, dogmáticas e imaginárias. Exemplo 3: Impotência sobre o Caráter e o Ser Enunciado: "Tu és uma pessoa horrível." A Realidade Pessoal: A estrutura biológica, a memória histórica, as reações químicas e as ações passadas do indivíduo que ouve este julgamento não sofrem qualquer modificação ontológica. A pessoa não se transforma subitamente num monstro físico. A alteração que se segue — a mágoa, a raiva ou a culpa — ocorre exclusivamente porque o recetador, dotado da capacidade de pensar, projeta a hipótese imaginária de "ser horrível" e reage emocionalmente a essa ilusão mental criada por ele próprio. 3. Injúrias, Tabus e o Conflito Criado pela Imaginação O verdadeiro problema humano surge quando nos debruçamos sobre enunciados desenhados para ferir, desumanizar ou insultar. É crucial analisar exemplos ofensivos para compreender a génese do conflito: a ofensa não está na palavra, mas no cenário imaginário que a mente valida como se fosse real. Exemplo Ofensivo 1: A Redução Taxonómica Enunciado: "Tu és um macaco!" Análise Material: O indivíduo atingido por esta injúria não perdeu os seus 46 cromossomas humanos, não viu o seu corpo cobrir-se de estrias pilosas primatas não-humanas, nem a sua espécie biológica mudou para Macaca mulatta ou Pan troglodytes . O seu código genético permanece 100% Homo sapiens . A pessoa **não se transformou num macaco** perante as palavras. O Problema Imaginado: Por que razão este enunciado causa indignação e dor social? Porque a mente humana recupera um histórico social de racismo, hierarquias de desumanização e projeções de inferioridade. A dor não vem de uma mutação física, mas da **capacidade da mente de imaginar a agressão estética e moral** contida no símbolo. Enunciado: "Tu és um parasita inútil, a tua existência é um lixo!" Análise Material: Os órgãos do indivíduo continuam a funcionar, o seu cérebro continua a processar oxigénio e o seu valor biológico permanece inalterado. A palavra "lixo" é uma categoria da gestão de resíduos sólidos humanos, inacessível como estado de matéria biológica viva. O Problema Imaginado: Se o recetador não aplicar o filtro do discernimento racional, a sua imaginação simula a rejeição social, a perda de utilidade e o desprezo dos seus pares, desencadeando respostas neuroquímicas de ansiedade e depressão perante uma pura abstração verbal. 4. A Racionalidade como Filtro entre a Verdade e a Ficção A verdadeira maturidade intelectual e a racionalidade radicam na faculdade de discriminar categoricamente entre o que é faticamente verdadeiro e o que é pura construção fabulada ou falsa, aprendendo a ignorar o falso e a acolher o verdadeiro . "A racionalidade está na capacidade de discernir sobre o que é verdadeiro ou falso, sabendo ignorar o que é falso e reconhecer o que é verdadeiro: Independentemente da cor, todos somos humanos e todos os humanos são animais." Estímulo Verbal (A Palavra) Fato Material / Científico A Armadilha do Imaginário A Resposta Racional "Esta raça é inferior." Todos os humanos partilham 99,9% do genoma; a variação de pigmentação é mera adaptação melânica à radiação UV. Imaginar hierarquias de sangue, superioridade moral e preconceitos históricos. Ignorar o falso: Rejeitar a premissa como erro científico e absurdo biológico. "Nós não somos animais, somos seres divinos purificados." O Homo sapiens é um animal vertebrado, mamífero, da ordem dos primatas, sujeito à biologia e à morte. Imaginar uma separação mística da natureza que justifica a destruição do ecossistema. Reconhecer o verdadeiro: Aceitar a nossa animalidade partilhada e a nossa igualdade biológica. "Tu és uma aberração para a natureza." A diversidade comportamental e biológica é uma constante observada em todas as espécies da biologia. Imaginar-se fora do ordem natural e sentir vergonha existencial. Ignorar o falso: Compreender a palavra como mero ruído ideológico sem adesão à realidade. 5. A Origem do Conflito: O Labirinto da Mente Pensante Se as palavras são impotentes, por que razão guerras foram travadas, duelos foram travados e vidas foram destruídas por causa de insultos ou heresias? A resposta reside inteiramente no **poder da imaginação humana**. A mente humana não é apenas um recetador passivo de dados; é uma máquina de simulação narrativa. Quando alguém ouve uma palavra ofensiva, o cérebro realiza as seguintes etapas em milissegundos: Descodificação Simbólica: O som transforma-se num conceito (ex.: a palavra "macaco" associada a um ser humano). Em 1867, a grande reforma judiciária portuguesa organiza uma polícia civil sob controlo das autoridades judiciais, com atributos de investigação penal — a matriz de tudo o que a PJ viria a ser. Ao contrário da Guarda Nacional Republicana, que nasce militar e cobre o território, esta polícia nasce administrativa e processual: existe para servir o inquérito, não para patrulhar. Essa diferença de berço explica a diferença de carácter que ainda hoje separa as duas instituições: o tigre dessa outra história é visível na rua da cidade; a serpente só se mostra quando o processo a chama. 1867 A reforma judiciária cria a polícia civil Sob direcção das autoridades judiciais nasce numa reorganização da justiça uma polícia de investigação penal com quadros civis — o embrião institucional da futura PJ, concentrada em Lisboa e Porto. 1936 A sombra política ganha corpo próprio O Estado Novo cria a PVDE, depois PIDE, separando a vigilância política da investigação comum. police: Home · index.html Technical Manual / Police Groups in Society Edition 1.0 · Promotional Reference · Interactive How Police Groups Work in Different Societies A technical-reference guide to the structure, activity, and evolution of police groups across societies — with animated examples and a graduated knowledge check. Read it top-to-bottom to earn each next level. How to use this manual This document is built like a technical manual. Each Level unlocks the next only when you answer its check. Real country examples are used throughout. Where a decision is framed as “bad,” the manual treats it as a class of failure common to multiple systems — outcomes of comparable quality — rather than a trophy for any one country. Level 1 · Concepts Unlocked Before comparing countries, learn the vocabulary. Continue to the questions below, then mark Validate Level 1 . 1) A “police group” in this manual means: Any organized body that performs policing functions — uniformed police, gendarmerie, constabulary, special forces with police roles, and oversight bodies that shape policing. Only the regular municipal police force of a city. Only armed officers on patrol. 2) “Police by consent” most closely describes: A model where legitimacy depends on public approval and police generally remain unarmed in routine work. A model where legitimacy depends on public approval and police generally remain unarmed in routine work (as historically in the UK and New Zealand). A model where police rule by decree without local input. 3) A “dual police” system is one where: Two distinct national forces share policing duties — for example a metropolitan police and a rural/gendarmerie force — plus municipal police. Police work is split between men and women. Police officers are forbidden to carry radios. Validate Level 1 Chapter 1 LEVEL 1 What a “police group” is — and is not In technical terms, a police group is a bounded organization with authority to apply coercive force under a legal framework, a defined jurisdiction, internal hierarchy, and accountability channels. The group may be called police, gendarmerie, constabulary, civil guard, or something else — the name is local, not universal. Core concepts Jurisdiction — the territory and subject-matter a group is empowered to act in. Hierarchy — the chain of command and rank structure. Function — what the group actually does: patrol, investigate, respond, detain, prevent. Consent / legitimacy — whether the public accepts the group’s right to act. Oversight — independent bodies that inspect, investigate, and discipline. Co-production — the extent to which policing relies on non-police actors (medics, social workers, community members). Concept map Four axes of comparison Every police group can be described along: (1) centralization , (2) armed vs. unarmed routine posture , (3) training depth , (4) oversight independence . These four axes explain most cross-country differences without reducing a country to a stereotype. Watch-out The “best police” trap No single system is universally “best.” Each trades off cost, speed, local knowledge, coercion, and accountability. A system that excels at corruption control may be criticized elsewhere for severity; a decentralized system may be flexible but uneven. Compare dimensions , not medals. Manual convention: when this text labels a decision a “bad decision,” it means a decision that fails its own stated objective and is structurally comparable to similar failures in other systems — it does not claim any country is uniquely bad. Equal weight across systems. Chapter 2 LEVEL 2 How police groups produce their activity Activity is not random. A group’s output — patrols, arrests, reports, stops, prevention — flows from four inputs and one feedback loop. Inputs What feeds the machine Budget & staffing set capacity. Legal mandate sets what is allowed. Data & intelligence set where attention goes. Training & doctrine set the style of action. Change any input and activity changes. Cycle The feedback loop Activity produces records (calls, crimes, stops). Records feed analysis. Analysis changes deployment. Deployment changes activity. The loop is where strategy becomes reality — or where it silently degrades. The activity stack (bottom to top) Layer What it is Example 1 · Reactivity Responding to calls and incidents as they arrive. UK 999/101 calls; US 911 dispatch; Japan koban local reports. 2 · Patrol & visibility Presence meant to deter and to gather local knowledge. Neighborhood beats; koban boxes; foot patrols; random vehicle stops (varies by country). 3 · Investigation Follow-up after an event, including forensics and interviews. Detective branches; specialized units; cross-border cooperation. 4 · Proactive / prevention Acting before harm using patterns, partnerships, and problem-solving. Community policing; intelligence-led deployment; problem-oriented projects (SARA). 5 · Strategic governance Policy, standards, training, oversight, funding choices. National standards bodies; independent complaints offices; academies; budget cycles. Animated cycle: calls → deployment → records → analysis → new deployment. Each society tilts the stack differently. The SARA loop — problem-oriented policing One widely used framework is SARA : S canning, A nalysis, R esponse, A ssessment. It is a decision model that keeps a team from acting on hunches alone. Scanning Spot the recurring problem What keeps happening? Which locations, times, victims, and repeat events form a pattern worth a project — not just one-off calls. Analysis Understand causes Look at the “problem triangle” — likely offender, suitable target, absence of capable guardian — plus environment and incentives. Response Design an intervention Not necessarily “more arrests.” Could be environmental change, partnership with housing/health, targeted deterrence, or removing a contributing condition. Assessment Did it work? Measure before/after on the problem you defined. If it didn’t help, revise. The loop is the point — not the single action. SARA loop animated: scan → analyze → respond → assess → back to scan. Level 2 · Activity Locked Answer the Level 2 check to unlock the country comparison. 1) Which best describes the SARA model? A ranking of officers. A four-step problem-solving cycle: Scanning, Analysis, Response, Assessment. A budgeting formula. 2) In a feedback loop, what turns activity into the next round of activity? Records and analysis that reshape deployment and priorities. Nothing — activity is purely instinctive. A single annual speech by the chief. Validate Level 2 Chapter 3 LEVEL 3 A real comparison: different police parties, different countries Here we compare real systems side-by-side. The goal is understanding , not ranking. Each system is a bundle of choices. United Kingdom — England & Wales Policing by consent, unarmed routine, regional forces Most officers do not carry firearms and historically rely on public approval. Policing is delivered by regional forces under national training/standards expectations; oversight is via the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which handles the most serious matters and sets complaint-handling standards. Good fit: legitimacy-driven, de-escalation culture, independent oversight. Trade-off: capacity strain, uneven local performance, firearm incidents require specially armed units. Japan Koban community policing, long training, high visibility Japan operates roughly 6,000 neighborhood police boxes (koban) staffed around the clock, embedding officers in daily community life — addressing lost-and-found, directions, minor disputes, and local crime prevention alongside law enforcement. Training and academy structure are comparatively long and formal. Good fit: local knowledge, prevention, low threshold for contact. Trade-off: historical debate about closeness of police-community ties and conformity pressure; success partly reflects broader social context. United States Many agencies, decentralized, armed, broad mandate The US has on the order of 18,000 law-enforcement agencies across local, state, and federal levels. Training length is comparatively short on average, and academies historically emphasize technical/firearm skills more than de-escalation and crisis intervention. Some agencies carry military-style equipment; funding is largely local. Good fit: local responsiveness, specialization, rapid innovation in some agencies. Trade-off: patchwork standards, broad mandates (including mental-health calls), higher lethal-encounter statistics than many peer democracies. France Dual national forces plus municipal police France has a dual structure: a National Police (Police nationale) for urban areas and a National Gendarmerie (Gendarmerie nationale) with a rural/military heritage, plus municipal police at the local level. This split is a classic “dual police” example. Good fit: clear national capacity, specialized jurisdiction split. Trade-off: coordination complexity between forces; public debate about protest policing and use-of-force norms. Germany Federal, state (Land) police, emphasis on restraint in firearms training Germany’s policing is organized at the state (Land) level, with federal police (Bundespolizei, BKA) for specific cross-cutting roles. Firearms training in Germany is commonly described as emphasizing avoidance of force. Police functions can be broad, including public-order and regulatory tasks. Good fit: federal flexibility, restraint-minded training posture, specialized federal units. Trade-off: coordination across Länder, varied local capacity. Singapore Centralized, technology-heavy, neighborhood centres, corruption-control focus The Singapore Police Force (SPF) is a centralized force under the Ministry of Home Affairs, organized with both staff and line functions. It developed a Neighbourhood Police Centre (NPC) model for local one-stop presence, pairs policing with broader corruption-control institutions and policy choices (pay, conditions, enforcement). Good fit: coordination, tech, corruption-control design. Trade-off: centralized model may generalize less easily; legitimacy and severity questions are debated by observers. Level 3 · Country comparison Locked Answer the Level 3 check to unlock the development and references section. 1) Which country is a textbook example of a “dual” national police structure (two national forces with different roles, plus municipal police)? France (National Police + National Gendarmerie + municipal police). Japan. New Zealand. 2) Which idea best matches “policing by consent”? Legitimacy rests on public approval; routine officers may be unarmed and rely on cooperation. Police command by personal authority alone. Consent is irrelevant; force defines legitimacy. 3) A “bad decision” in policing, in this manual’s terms, is: A trophy that belongs to one country only. A failure class (poor escalation, weak accountability, misaligned mandate, or misuse of data) that can occur in many systems and is weighed equally across them. Anything any police ever do. Validate Level 3 Chapter 4 LEVEL 4 Developing activity: how a police group improves Improvement is not a slogan. It is a set of interventions that change inputs and the feedback loop. Below are techniques used (with variation) across societies, followed by the real example of a “bad decision” class and how to avoid it. Improvement levers Lever What it changes Real-world flavour Longer, deeper training Decision quality under stress; de-escalation; legal/ethical judgment. Several European systems train recruits for years and pair academy study with practice; some include degree-level study. Problem-oriented projects (SARA) Shifts from “more of the same” to tailored interventions. Local teams targeting a recurring hotspot or repeat harm with analysis and follow-up assessment. Intelligence-led deployment Prioritization informed by analysis, not only the loudest call. Data-informed resource targeting, with safeguards against bias and over-policing. Co-production / alternative responders Reduces armed escalation by sending the right responder. Unarmed crisis responders for mental-health calls; community support officers handling low-level matters; CAHOOTS-style programs. Independent oversight Improves accountability and public confidence. Watchdog bodies that investigate serious matters and set complaint standards; external audit of use-of-force. Transparency & data Makes activity visible and debatable. Published stop/arrest/use-of-force data; regular public reporting; open methodology. Corruption-control design Reduces rent-seeking and abuse. Pay/conditions, clear anti-corruption institutions, enforcement, and prevention — an integrated approach rather than one silver bullet. Real example: a bad-decision class and why it is equal across systems Consider “escalate-by-default in low-risk encounters.” If routine encounters are handled by maximizing coercion rather than de-escalation, several things happen at once: public trust falls, the encounter set expands (more people are pulled into conflict), and the group spends capacity on avoidable conflict instead of prevention. This is a decision class , not a country trophy. Similar failures can arise wherever doctrine, training, incentives, or data practices push officers toward escalation, silence, or secrecy. The manual treats the quality of the failure as comparable across systems and asks: what input produced it, and which lever would change it? Animated “improvement flywheel”: better training → better decisions → less avoidable conflict → more capacity for prevention → more trust. How to read a country’s police group (a short method) Step 1 Name the group(s) and their jurisdiction. Step 2 State the default armed/unarmed posture and use-of-force rules. Step 3 Identify training length/emphasis and doctrine. Step 4 Identify oversight and accountability channels. Step 5 Identify where co-production and alternative responders sit. Step 6 Read the feedback loop: what data is collected, who sees it, and how it changes deployment. Promotional note: this manual is intended to promote clear, comparative understanding of police groups — the discipline of comparing real systems honestly, without turning any country into a moral mascot.
